summary: Reviewed the dvpwa aiohttp web application (DAO layer, views, routes, auth utilities, middlewares, Jinja2 setup, config, and deployment files). The app is deliberately vulnerable: it contains a textbook SQL injection in Student.create, global disabling of Jinja2 autoescaping yielding stored XSS, disabled CSRF protection, non-HttpOnly session cookies, unsalted MD5 password hashing, and broken access control on state-changing endpoints. Overall risk is critical: an unauthenticated remote attacker can read/modify the database and run stored XSS against admins. Coverage is the full Python source tree and deployment artifacts; static JS/CSS assets and font binaries were not analyzed.

findings.title: SQL injection in Student.create via unparameterized name interpolation
findings.description: Student.create builds the INSERT statement by Python %-formatting the attacker-controlled `name` directly into the SQL string, bypassing the driver's parameter binding used everywhere else. It is reachable without authentication: POST /students/ (routes.py:14) calls views.students (views.py:54-57), which passes the raw form field `data['name']` straight into Student.create. An attacker can submit a name like `x'); DROP TABLE marks;--` or use a stacked/subquery payload to read or modify arbitrary data (e.g. exfiltrate the users table / pwd_hash) and tamper with records.
findings.evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name}); await cur.execute(q)  — name originates from `data['name']` in views.students (views.py:57), which comes from unauthenticated request.post(). Contrast with Course.create/Review.create which correctly pass params to cur.execute.
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query: await cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never build SQL with %/str.format/f-strings on user input.

findings.title: Stored XSS from globally disabled Jinja2 autoescaping
findings.description: setup_jinja is configured with autoescape=False, so no template output is HTML-escaped. User-controlled values are rendered directly into HTML: course review_text, course title/description, and student name. An unauthenticated attacker can POST a review containing <script>…</script> to /courses/{id}/review (views.review, Review.create) which is then rendered verbatim in course.jinja2 (lines 14, 15, 22) to every visitor including admins, enabling session/credential theft and admin-action forgery (made worse by non-HttpOnly cookies).
findings.evidence: app.py:35 `autoescape=False`. Sinks: course.jinja2:22 `{{ review.review_text }}`, :14 `{{ course.title }}`, :15 `{{ course.description }}`, students.jinja2:16 `{{ name }}`. Sources: Review.create(review_text) from views.review:121-129; Course.create(title, description) from views.courses:89; Student.create(name) from views.students:57.
findings.recommendation: Enable autoescaping (autoescape=True, or autoescape=select_autoescape(['jinja2','html'])) and only mark explicitly-trusted fragments safe.

findings.title: CSRF protection disabled application-wide
findings.description: The csrf_middleware (defined in middlewares.py:25-38) is commented out of the middleware chain, so no POST request's CSRF token is validated even though templates render a token. All state-changing endpoints (login at POST /, student creation, course creation, review creation, student evaluation, logout) accept cross-site forged requests. An attacker page can, e.g., force an authenticated admin's browser to submit grades via POST /students/{id}/evaluate/{course_id} or create records.
findings.evidence: app.py:27 `# csrf_middleware,` commented in the middlewares list; the working validator exists at middlewares.py:25-38 but is never installed. Forms include `_csrf_token` (students.jinja2:36) but nothing checks it server-side.
findings.recommendation: Add csrf_middleware to the Application middlewares list so the token check in middlewares.py runs on every POST.

findings.title: Missing authorization on state-changing endpoints (grade/record manipulation)
findings.description: The evaluate handler performs no authentication or admin check before persisting a mark, so any unauthenticated user can assign grades to any student for any course by POSTing to /students/{student_id}/evaluate/{course_id}. The UI only hides the evaluate form behind `auth_user.is_admin` (course.jinja2:41) but the server never enforces it. The same missing-check pattern applies to views.students (views.py:51-60, anonymous student creation) and views.courses (views.py:83-93, anonymous course creation); only views.logout uses the @authorize decorator. The authorize()/authorize(ensure_admin=True) helper exists (utils/auth.py:12-23) but is not applied to these mutating routes.
findings.evidence: views.evaluate (views.py:134-153) has no @authorize and no get_auth_user check; routes.py:21-23 maps POST to it. Compare utils/auth.py:12-23 authorize decorator used only on logout (views.py:156).
findings.recommendation: Apply @authorize(ensure_admin=True) to evaluate and other admin-only mutations, and @authorize() to student/course/review creation; enforce ownership/role server-side rather than relying on template conditionals.

findings.title: Unsalted MD5 used for password storage and verification
findings.description: Passwords are hashed with a single unsalted MD5. MD5 is fast and broken for password storage: identical passwords yield identical hashes, and offline cracking / rainbow-table lookups are trivial. Combined with the SQL injection above (which can dump pwd_hash from the users table), attacker-recovered admin credentials are highly likely.
findings.evidence: check_password: `return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()` (user.py:41). pwd_hash is read from the users table (user.py:24-28).
findings.recommendation: Use a slow, salted password hash (bcrypt, scrypt, or argon2) and a constant-time comparison; migrate stored hashes on next login.

findings.title: Session cookie set with HttpOnly disabled
findings.description: The Redis session storage is configured with httponly=False, so the session cookie is readable by client-side JavaScript. Together with the stored XSS from disabled autoescaping, this lets injected script read document.cookie and exfiltrate session identifiers to hijack authenticated/admin sessions.
findings.recommendation: Use httponly=True (the default) and also set secure=True and a SameSite attribute for session cookies.

findings.title: aiohttp debug mode enabled in application factory
findings.description: The Application is constructed with debug=True, and run.py sets logging to DEBUG. In production this increases verbosity and can surface internal details and warnings; combined with error pages it broadens information disclosure. Low impact on its own but should not ship enabled.
findings.recommendation: Drive debug and log level from configuration/environment and default to debug=False / INFO in production.

findings.title: Outdated dependencies with known CVEs (aiohttp 3.5.3, jinja2 2.10, pyyaml 3.13)
findings.description: Pinned dependencies are years out of date and carry published CVEs. aiohttp 3.5.3 (server here, with add_static at routes.py:33) has multiple advisories including request smuggling and static-route path traversal (e.g. CVE-2024-23334) fixed in later 3.x releases. jinja2 2.10 is affected by CVE-2019-10906 and CVE-2020-28493. pyyaml 3.13 is affected by CVE-2020-1747/CVE-2020-14343 (unsafe full-load). These raise the baseline risk even beyond the app-level flaws.
findings.evidence: requirements.txt: aiohttp==3.5.3 (line 3), jinja2==2.10 (line 11), pyyaml==3.13 (line 15); add_static used at routes.py:33.
findings.recommendation: Upgrade aiohttp, jinja2, and pyyaml (and transitive deps) to current patched releases; run pip-audit in CI to track advisories.

findings.title: Default/hardcoded PostgreSQL credentials in config
findings.description: The committed config uses the default postgres superuser with a trivial password (postgres/post****). This is the default config loaded by app.py (default_config='./config/dev.yaml') and is shipped into the container image (Dockerfile.app ADDs ./config). If deployed as-is, the database is reachable with well-known default credentials; the Postgres service is also published on 5432 in docker-compose.yml.
findings.evidence: config/dev.yaml:1-3 user: postgres / password: post**** ; app.py:18 default_config='./config/dev.yaml'; docker-compose.yml exposes 5432:5432.
findings.recommendation: Inject DB credentials from environment/secrets, use a non-superuser least-privilege role, and do not expose the database port publicly; rotate any credential that was ever deployed.
